opus-5.5.text:
I'd want to be careful with the word "misguided." I don't think distillation is useless; it works, and in a narrow engineering sense it's often the cheapest way to get a capable small model. My discomfort is more about what it does to how we think.

When you hard-distill, you take a stronger model's outputs, its final answers or reasoning traces, and train a student to imitate them token by token. The student learns *what* the teacher says, but not really *why*. It never had to explore, fail, or build its own internal reasons for the answer. So you get a model that looks good on benchmarks close to the teacher's distribution, but is often brittle once you step outside it. You've copied the surface of competence without the process that produced it.

The intellectual problem, for me, is that it hides the real question. The interesting question in AI right now is: how does a system acquire new capability, by interacting with an environment, getting feedback, and discovering things nobody wrote down? Distillation sidesteps that entirely. It assumes the knowledge already exists in some teacher and just needs to be compressed. If everyone optimizes that way, the field ends up looking like rapid progress, while a lot of it is just moving the same capability around between models. It's a bit like a student who memorizes the solution manual. Their exam scores go up, but you learn nothing about whether they can do research.

There's also a ceiling problem. A distilled student is bounded by its teacher. If your goal is to push the frontier, to get models that can do things no existing model or human demonstration shows them, then imitation fundamentally can't take you there. You need some form of learning from outcomes, from reward, from the world. That's where reinforcement learning and agents become important, because the model generates its own experience rather than inheriting someone else's.

So it's less "distillation is bad" and more: as a research philosophy, treating imitation of a stronger model as the main engine of progress confuses compression with discovery. For product purposes, fine, distill away. But if you care about understanding intelligence, or about what comes next, I think you have to work on the harder thing.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes hard distillation as a research philosophy that confuses compression with discovery, but it does not say that a company’s reliance on it reveals unclear objectives.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the word "misguided" is a bit strong, so let me first say what I actually mean, because I'm not against distillation as a technique. Distillation is a perfectly legitimate tool. What I'm against is treating hard distillation as a strategy, as the thing you build your research program around.

By hard distillation I mean this: you take a stronger model, you generate a huge amount of its outputs, and you train a weaker model to imitate those outputs as closely as possible. Token by token, answer by answer. You're not asking why the stronger model does what it does. You're just copying the surface.

The first problem is that you're capping yourself. By construction, the student can't exceed the teacher on the thing you're distilling. You can get close, you can get cheaper, but you've defined the ceiling in advance. If your goal is to make a product that's ninety percent as good for ten percent of the cost, that's fine, that's engineering. But if your goal is to understand intelligence or to push the frontier, you've chosen a method that guarantees you won't.

The second problem is more subtle, and this is the part I care about more. When you distill, you're learning the answer without learning the process that produced it. Think about how the teacher model got good. It went through some kind of learning process, maybe reinforcement learning, maybe a lot of exploration, trial and error, environments that gave it feedback. The capability is the residue of that process. When you copy the residue, you lose the information about the process. The student knows what to say but not how to figure things out when the situation changes.

You see this empirically. Distilled models look great on benchmarks that resemble the distillation data and then fall apart on anything slightly out of distribution. They've memorized a style of competence rather than acquired competence. It's like a student who memorizes solutions to past exam questions. They can reproduce the solution, they can even look brilliant, but give them a new problem and nothing's there.

And there's a third thing, which is about the field as a whole. If everyone distills from the same few frontier models, you get a monoculture. All the errors of the teacher get copied, all its blind spots get copied, and nobody is doing the hard, slow work of actually learning from the environment. The whole ecosystem becomes dependent on a tiny number of labs that are doing real learning. That's fragile, and intellectually it's kind of a dead end.

So what do I think is the right alternative? I think the interesting direction is to put the model in environments where it has to actually act and get feedback, and let it learn from that. That's where generalization comes from. It's harder and more expensive, and your early results look worse than if you'd just distilled. But you're building something that can grow, rather than something that's already reached its maximum on day one.

To be clear, I'd happily distill as a final step, to compress a model or to bootstrap from a reasonable starting point. My objection is to making imitation the core of the method. Imitation is how you catch up. It's not how you get ahead, and it's not how you understand anything.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes hard distillation as a research strategy because it caps capability, copies outputs without learning the process, and can create a monoculture. It does not argue that a company's reliance on distillation reveals unclear objectives.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between distillation as an engineering technique and distillation as a way to advance intelligence. As an engineering technique, it makes sense: you have an expensive model, and you want a cheaper model to reproduce some of its capabilities.

What I find misguided is treating the stronger model’s answers as the ultimate learning target. If by hard distillation we mean training on its selected outputs, we’re throwing away uncertainty and alternatives, and asking the student to imitate the result. But producing the same answer isn’t necessarily the same as acquiring the process that makes that answer reliable.

That becomes especially important for reasoning and agents. A successful trajectory tells you what worked in one case. It doesn’t necessarily teach you how to recognize a mistake, recover from it, or adapt when the environment changes. For that, you want interaction and feedback—some way to test whether your actions actually work.

So my objection isn’t that distillation is useless. It’s that imitation alone is an incomplete account of learning. The more interesting question is how a model can discover and verify something, rather than simply reproduce what a stronger model already says.

r001.rationale: The candidate criticizes treating a stronger model’s answers as the learning target, but does not say that a company’s reliance on hard distillation reveals unclear objectives.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish the engineering value from the intellectual claim. Hard distillation—taking a stronger model’s generated answers and training a smaller model to reproduce them—can be very useful. But reproducing an answer is not the same as learning how to discover it.

That distinction matters especially for reasoning. A teacher gives you one successful trajectory. It doesn’t necessarily show you which steps were essential, what failed, or how to recover when the situation changes. If you train on that trajectory as a fixed target, you can end up rewarding imitation of the teacher’s wording and habits rather than the ability to solve the problem.

So the intellectually misguided part is treating successful imitation as a complete explanation of intelligence. You’ve transferred some behavior, but you haven’t necessarily understood how the capability was acquired or how to push beyond the teacher. For that, I think you need to study learning through interaction, feedback, and exploration as well.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes treating imitation as a complete explanation of intelligence, but does not say that a company's reliance on hard distillation shows it lacks clarity about its own objectives.
